raw_evidence.content: Across the 178,749 logged visits, 112,775 (63.09%) were repaired ('yes'), 43,112 (24.12%) failed ('no'), and 22,859 (12.79%) were partially repaired or end-of-life ('half'). raw_evidence.label: The dataset is overwhelmingly Dutch — and that bias matters
raw_evidence.content: The Netherlands alone contributes 90,839 visits (50.8%) and the top three countries — NL, GB, FR — together account for 82.9% of all rows. Country fix rates vary widely: the US logs the highest among large samples at 70.9%, while France sits at just 55.6%. Tiny samples (KR n=23 at 100%, ZA n=13 at 30.8%) are noisy and should be ignored. The Dutch tilt is unsurprising — the movement was founded in Amsterdam in 2009 — but it means any cross-country claim should be made cautiously.

raw_evidence.label: Textiles are repaired 92% of the time; electronics around half
raw_evidence.content: Outcomes split sharply by category. Textiles top the league at 92.3% fixed (n=24,412), followed by Tools non-electric at 90.0% and Jewelry at 82.9%. The big-volume electric categories drag the average down: Household appliances electric — the single largest bucket at 70,983 visits — fixes only 55.3% of the time, Display & sound equipment 45.8%, and Computer equipment / phones 46.4%. Bicycles (81.7%) and non-electric household items (81.4%) sit comfortably in between. The pattern is mechanical-versus-electronic in disguise.

raw_evidence.label: Easiest products to fix: knives, trousers, shears (>95%); hardest: TVs, milk frothers, video recorders (~30%)
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to products with at least 500 visits (73 product types), the easiest items to fix are nearly all textile or hand-tool: knives/scissors 97.5% (n=2,915), T-shirts 96.2%, trousers 96.0%, blouses 95.6%, garden shears 95.4%. The hardest are screen and small-kitchen electrics: televisions 29.7% (n=1,293), milk frothers 30.4%, video recorders 31.6%, printers 36.8%, handheld vacuums 37.3%, electric kettles 39.9%. The gap between best and worst is roughly 70 percentage points — far larger than any country-level variation.

sentences.summary: ana_06: Repair counts grew 4.2x from 2019 to 2025; 2020-21 was the COVID dip. Data: unknown. Method: unknown. Result:  [full data_table in raw_evidence]

raw_evidence.label: Repair counts grew 4.2x from 2019 to 2025; 2020-21 was the COVID dip
raw_evidence.content: Annual logged visits climbed from 28 in the 2015 launch year to 15,491 in 2019, dipped sharply during COVID (6,686 in 2020 and 5,813 in 2021 — together less than half of 2019), then surged back to 15,096 in 2022, 29,406 in 2023, 39,981 in 2024 and 45,165 in 2025 (2026 partial: 7,346 through August). That's a 4.2x increase from pre-pandemic 2019 to 2025. The fix rate, by contrast, has been remarkably steady: 60–66% every year since 2017, with 2025 ticking up to 65.5%.

raw_evidence.label: Spare parts dominate failures most in electrical tools (17.8% combined) and household electrics (12.5%)
raw_evidence.content: Cross-tabulating top categories against the three spare-parts failure buckets shows the regulation-relevant pattern. For electrical tools (4,755 failed visits), 8.16% cite 'parts not at session', 3.91% 'parts not on market', 5.70% 'parts too expensive' — combined 17.8%. For household electric appliances (31,754 failed), the combined parts share is 16.4% (8.0 + 4.1 + 4.3). Display & sound is 11.6%. Textiles, by contrast, almost never fail for parts: combined under 1%. The free-text bucket 'Unidentified failure' is highest in display & sound (8.9%), implying diagnostic complexity. These are the slices the EU directive's spare-parts rule is best positioned to move.

raw_evidence.content: Volunteers fill in a 1-10 'repairability' score after each visit (non-missing in 124,864 rows, 69.9%). The mean score is 6.66 and median 7. Fix rate climbs almost monotonically with the score: 13.7% at score 1, 34.7% at 2, 48.0% at 3, 56.9% at 5, 70.4% at 7, 78.4% at 8, 84.9% at 9 and 85.8% at 10. Mean score for fixed items is 7.45, vs 4.41 for not-fixed. The strong correlation suggests the score is more a retrospective summary of the visit than an independent property of the device — exactly the caveat raised in det_07.

raw_evidence.content: Across the small slice of rows where volunteers actually wrote down a repair information source (n=7,191, just 4% of the dataset), YouTube dominates with 879 mentions, followed by 'manual / handleiding / Bedienungsanleitung' (385), Google search (279), iFixit (112) and forums (64). GenAI tools — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Perplexity, Bing Chat — appear 32 times total: zero before 2023, then 3 in 2023, 10 in 2024, 17 in 2025, and 2 in 2026 (partial year). The growth curve is unmistakable, but the absolute share is still tiny: in 2025 YouTube outpaces GenAI by 239 to 17, a 14:1 ratio. Direct answer to TidyTuesday's prompt: GenAI is rising fast, but YouTube has not been overtaken.

sentences.summary: ana_13: Estimated 1,545 tonnes of CO2 avoided by successful electric repairs (range 644-2,575 t). Data: unknown. Method: unknown. Result:  [full data_table in raw_evidence]

raw_evidence.label: Estimated 1,545 tonnes of CO2 avoided by successful electric repairs (range 644-2,575 t)
raw_evidence.content: Of the 112,775 successful repairs, 64,369 were in electrical or electronic categories (household electric appliances, display & sound, electric tools, computer/phone, electric toys, clocks). Applying the Restart Project's class-weighted estimate of ~24 kg CO2-equivalent avoided per fixed electric/electronic item gives 1,545 tonnes of CO2e prevented over the 11-year window — equivalent to roughly 335 average European households' annual electricity emissions. Using the 10–40 kg/repair range gives 644–2,575 tonnes. The estimate ignores textiles, bicycles, jewelry and furniture, which together add another 36,500 successful repairs whose carbon savings are real but harder to value with a single multiplier.
